item.content:encoded:
The Swiss Centre of Expertise in Life Course Research (LIVES) has opened applications for its next cohort of doctoral researchers, offering early-stage PhD candidates the opportunity to join an internationally oriented and interdisciplinary doctoral programme focused on life course and lifespan research.

The LIVES Doctoral Programme is designed for researchers whose doctoral projects examine how people’s lives develop and change over time, including issues surrounding education, employment, health, ageing, social transitions, family experiences, public policy, and other factors that influence individual and collective life trajectories.

The programme has been running since 2012 and has supported more than 130 PhD graduates. For the upcoming cohort, LIVES is inviting applications from eligible doctoral students who want to strengthen their theoretical knowledge, methodological expertise, interdisciplinary research skills, and academic networks.

The new cohort will run from December 2026 to February 2029, with activities taking place at the University of Geneva and the University of Lausanne in Switzerland.

Opportunity Overview

The LIVES Doctoral Programme provides structured doctoral training for PhD candidates whose research is connected to the study of life courses and human development across time.

Rather than being a conventional PhD scholarship or a standalone doctoral degree, the programme functions as an additional specialised training programme that doctoral candidates can undertake alongside their existing disciplinary PhD training.

This makes it particularly valuable for researchers who are already enrolled in doctoral programmes and want to develop stronger expertise in life course theory, longitudinal research, interdisciplinary approaches, and advanced methodological techniques.

Key details at a glance

  • Programme: LIVES Doctoral Programme
  • Cohort: December 2026 – February 2029
  • Host: Swiss Centre of Expertise in Life Course Research (LIVES)
  • Locations: University of Geneva and University of Lausanne, Switzerland
  • Opportunity type: Doctoral training programme
  • Target applicants: Early-stage PhD/doctoral students
  • Research focus: Life course and lifespan research
  • Eligible fields: Social sciences, psychology, health sciences and related disciplines
  • Study/research format: In-person workshops, training sessions and academic events
  • English requirement: Minimum B2 level
  • Application deadline: 30 September 2026
  • Admissions decision: No later than the end of October 2026
  • Programme start: December 2026

What Is the LIVES Doctoral Programme?

The LIVES Doctoral Programme is a specialised interdisciplinary programme developed to support doctoral researchers studying life course processes.

The programme recognises that important outcomes in people’s lives are often shaped by events and experiences occurring at different points throughout their lives. Researchers may therefore need approaches that can connect childhood experiences, education, employment, health, family life, ageing, social change and other transitions across time.

LIVES brings together doctoral researchers working on these kinds of questions and provides them with opportunities to receive training from specialists, exchange ideas with other PhD candidates and obtain feedback from experienced researchers.

The programme also places considerable emphasis on longitudinal methods and life course analysis, making it particularly relevant to researchers working with data that follows people, groups or populations over extended periods.

Who Should Apply?

The programme is aimed at early-stage doctoral students whose PhD research has a clear life course or lifespan perspective.

Potential applicants may be researching a wide variety of topics. What matters most is the connection between the doctoral project and life course research.

Applicants may come from disciplines such as:

  • Sociology
  • Demography
  • Psychology
  • Epidemiology
  • Economics
  • Political Science
  • Neuroscience
  • History
  • Gender Studies
  • Health sciences
  • Other related disciplines

The programme is interdisciplinary, meaning that applicants do not necessarily need to come from one specific academic department.

Examples of Eligible Research Topics

LIVES provides several examples of research areas that can fit within its programme.

1. Early-Life Events and Later Outcomes

Research may investigate how experiences during childhood, adolescence or other early stages of life affect outcomes later in life.

For example, a doctoral researcher could study how childhood socioeconomic circumstances influence educational achievement, employment opportunities, health or social mobility later in adulthood.

2. Life Trajectories Across Different Domains

Applicants may study how people’s trajectories develop across different areas of life.

Possible domains include:

  • Education
  • Employment
  • Health
  • Family
  • Social relationships
  • Economic circumstances
  • Migration
  • Ageing

Such research can examine how developments in one area of life interact with developments in another.

3. Turning Points and Transitions

Life course research can also focus on major transitions and turning points in individual biographies.

Examples could include:

  • Transition from school to work
  • Marriage or partnership
  • Parenthood
  • Retirement
  • Migration
  • Career changes
  • Major health events
  • Educational transitions

Researchers may investigate what causes these transitions and how they affect people’s subsequent trajectories.

4. Accumulation and Depletion Across the Life Span

The programme also welcomes research examining how advantages and disadvantages accumulate or diminish over time.

This could involve studying how socioeconomic advantage, educational opportunities, health conditions or social resources build up across different stages of life.

5. Longitudinal Methods and Data Analysis

Applicants whose projects involve longitudinal datasets and methods may find the programme particularly relevant.

Longitudinal research allows researchers to examine change over time rather than relying solely on observations from a single point.

6. Changing Social Norms Around Age and Ageing

Another potential area concerns changing attitudes, expectations and social norms surrounding age and ageing.

Researchers could examine how societies understand different stages of life and how these expectations change over generations.

7. Life Course Research and Public Policy

The programme also welcomes research examining how life course concepts can contribute to public policy.

This could include research into policies affecting education, employment, healthcare, ageing, family life, social protection or other areas of public policy.

Programme Structure

The LIVES Doctoral Programme is organised over approximately two years and combines theoretical training, methodological workshops, doctoral presentations and individual academic feedback.

Participants are expected to attend a number of activities throughout the programme.

The structure includes four intensive sessions on theories and concepts in life course research.

Each theoretical session lasts approximately two to three days and is designed to strengthen participants’ understanding of the conceptual foundations of life course research.

The programme also provides four methodological workshops focusing on longitudinal and life course analysis.

These workshops last approximately two to four days and are intended to develop participants’ ability to apply appropriate methods to life course research.

LIVES Doctoriales

A particularly important part of the programme is the LIVES Doctoriales.

Two annual Doctoriales are organised during the programme. These provide PhD candidates with an opportunity to present their research to senior scholars and receive expert feedback.

Presenting doctoral research in this setting can help researchers identify weaknesses, refine research questions, improve theoretical frameworks and strengthen methodological approaches.

It also provides valuable experience in communicating academic research to an expert audience.

Individual Expert Feedback

Participants also receive an individual feedback session.

During this session, doctoral researchers have the opportunity to discuss and exchange ideas about their research with an invited expert.

This personalised academic interaction can be particularly useful when a researcher is trying to address a difficult theoretical, methodological or conceptual issue within their thesis.

Commitment Required from Participants

Applicants should understand that joining the LIVES Doctoral Programme requires an active commitment to participation.

Participants are expected to attend at least 13 days of their choice from the eight doctoral workshops.

The programme also identifies certain activities as compulsory.

According to the call, Session 1 and the two LIVES Doctoriales are compulsory, and selected workshops and Doctoriales must be attended in person.

The programme is designed to complement, rather than replace, a participant’s existing disciplinary doctoral training.

PhD candidates who want to undertake LIVES training alongside their disciplinary training are explicitly welcome.

For example, a doctoral researcher may continue specialised training in areas such as social psychology, neuroscience or another discipline while participating in the LIVES programme.

Certificates and ECTS Credits

Participants can receive certificates of attendance for the programme modules.

The certificates include the corresponding number of ECTS credits, providing formal recognition of the training completed through the programme.

This can be useful for doctoral researchers who need evidence of additional academic training as part of their doctoral development.

Financial Support for Participants

The programme provides financial assistance to support participation, although applicants should note that this is not presented as a full doctoral scholarship covering all living and study expenses.

Support for Swiss-Based PhD Candidates

For PhD candidates based in Switzerland, travel expenses are reimbursed based on the cost of a half-fare second-class ticket.

Support for International PhD Candidates

International PhD candidates can receive financial assistance for travel of up to CHF 200 per session, for a maximum of five sessions.

This means eligible international participants could potentially receive up to CHF 1,000 in travel support across five sessions, subject to the programme’s applicable conditions.

Accommodation Support

LIVES also indicates that accommodation subsidies are available for a limited number of students.

International applicants who require accommodation assistance should contact the programme for further information.

Applicants from outside Switzerland are specifically asked in the application form whether they wish to request financial assistance for accommodation.

Meals and Breaks

The programme also provides some meal-related support.

During workshops, lunch breaks are covered.

During the LIVES Doctoriales, lunch and coffee breaks are covered.

Applicants should nevertheless carefully review the programme’s financial arrangements and contact LIVES if they require clarification regarding expenses that are not specifically listed as covered.

Eligibility Requirements

Applicants must satisfy several conditions before applying.

1. Your PhD Must Have a Life Course or Life Span Perspective

The doctoral thesis must incorporate a life course or lifespan perspective.

This is one of the most important eligibility requirements.

Simply being a doctoral student in a social science or health-related field is not enough. The research itself should meaningfully engage with life course or lifespan concepts.

2. Academic Discipline

The doctoral research should have a disciplinary background in an eligible or related field.

The call specifically mentions:

  • Sociology
  • Demography
  • Psychology
  • Epidemiology
  • Economics
  • Political Science
  • Neuroscience
  • History
  • Gender Studies

Related fields may also be considered where the doctoral project has a clear connection to life course research.

3. Existing Academic Affiliation

Applicants must already be affiliated with an academic institution.

This means the programme is intended for people who are already doctoral candidates rather than individuals who are merely planning to start a PhD in the future.

An official document confirming academic affiliation must be submitted with the application.

4. PhD Funding

The PhD thesis must be funded for the length of the doctoral programme.

Funding can come from:

  • An academic institution; or
  • Third-party funding.

Applicants should therefore ensure that their existing doctoral funding arrangement covers the required period.

5. English Language Ability

Applicants must be able to speak and write English fluently.

The minimum stated level is B2.

Because the programme involves workshops, academic presentations, discussions and written research materials, applicants should be comfortable communicating their research in English.

Where Can Applicants Be Based?

The programme is open to doctoral students based in Switzerland and Europe.

The call does not specify a particular racial, ethnic or nationality restriction.

Therefore, eligibility is primarily determined by the applicant’s academic status, institutional affiliation, research topic, funding and geographical location rather than race.

International applicants outside Switzerland can receive certain travel assistance, subject to the programme’s funding conditions.

Required Application Documents

Applicants must submit several supporting documents alongside the application form.

1. Cover Letter

Applicants must provide a cover letter explaining their motivation for joining the LIVES Doctoral Programme.

The letter should clearly explain:

  • Why the applicant wants to participate
  • How their PhD research relates to life course research
  • What they hope to gain from the programme
  • How the programme complements their existing doctoral training
  • Why the applicant would contribute meaningfully to the LIVES doctoral community

2. Curriculum Vitae

A CV must be submitted.

The CV should clearly present the applicant’s academic background, research experience, publications where applicable, professional experience, methodological skills, conferences and other relevant achievements.

3. PhD Project Title and Abstract

Applicants must provide the title and an abstract of their PhD project, with the abstract being approximately 500 words maximum.

This section should clearly communicate the research question, objectives, theoretical approach, methodology and relevance of the research to life course or lifespan studies.

4. Supervisor Recommendation Letter

Applicants must submit a one-page letter of support from their PhD supervisor or supervisors.

The recommendation should demonstrate the supervisor’s support for the applicant’s participation and establish the relevance of the LIVES programme to the doctoral research.

5. Official Academic Affiliation Document

Applicants must provide an official document certifying their affiliation with an academic institution.

This is important because applicants must already be affiliated with an academic institution to qualify.

Application Form Information

The online application form requests several pieces of information from candidates.

Applicants should be prepared to provide:

  • First name
  • Last name
  • Institutional email
  • Postal address
  • City
  • Postal code
  • Country
  • Academic institution
  • Discipline
  • Source of PhD funding
  • Name of PhD supervisor
  • Supervisor’s email address

Applicants must also upload their supporting documents.

The system allows up to 10 files, with a maximum total file size of 50 MB.

Accepted file formats include:

  • TXT
  • RTF
  • PDF
  • DOC
  • DOCX
  • ODT
  • PPT
  • PPTX
  • ODP
  • XLS
  • XLSX
  • ODS

After uploading the documents, applicants are instructed to check the boxes corresponding to the documents that should be submitted with their application.

Accommodation Assistance for International Applicants

Applicants from outside Switzerland will be asked whether they want to request financial assistance for accommodation.

The form provides two options:

  • Yes
  • No

Applicants who require accommodation assistance should indicate this during the application process and may also contact the programme for additional information about eligibility and available subsidies.

Application Deadline

The deadline to apply for the LIVES Doctoral Programme is:

30 September 2026

Applicants should avoid waiting until the final day to submit their materials.

Because the application requires multiple supporting documents, including a supervisor recommendation letter and official proof of academic affiliation, candidates should begin preparing their applications well before the deadline.

What Happens After Applying?

The admissions process is expected to be completed relatively soon after the deadline.

According to LIVES, admission decisions will be confirmed no later than the end of October 2026.

The new cohort is scheduled to begin in December 2026.

Successful applicants will subsequently sign an agreement involving:

  • The PhD candidate
  • Their supervisor or supervisors
  • The LIVES Doctoral Programme

This agreement formalises participation in the programme.

Why This Programme Could Be Valuable for PhD Researchers

The LIVES Doctoral Programme offers several potential academic and professional advantages.

Interdisciplinary Training

Life course research often crosses disciplinary boundaries. The programme brings together researchers from different academic backgrounds, allowing participants to encounter theories and methods beyond their primary discipline.

Advanced Methodological Skills

The methodological workshops focus on longitudinal and life course analysis, which can strengthen a researcher’s ability to analyse changes and developments over time.

Expert Academic Feedback

Participants have opportunities to present their research to senior scholars and receive specialised feedback.

This can be extremely valuable during the early stages of a PhD, when research questions, theoretical frameworks and methodologies are still being refined.

International Academic Network

The programme creates a community of international PhD researchers working on related questions.

Building relationships with other doctoral researchers can lead to future collaborations, research exchanges, conference opportunities and broader academic networks.

Exposure to Leading Life Course Research

Participants can deepen their understanding of life course theories, concepts and research methods through structured sessions and workshops.

Formal Recognition

Certificates and ECTS credits provide formal recognition of participation in the programme’s training modules.

Important Considerations Before Applying

Applicants should carefully assess whether the programme fits their current doctoral situation.

First, this is not an opportunity for someone who has not yet started a PhD. The applicant must already be affiliated with an academic institution.

Second, the PhD must be funded for the duration of the programme.

Third, the research must genuinely incorporate a life course or lifespan perspective. Applicants should therefore avoid presenting a project that only has a superficial connection to the topic.

Fourth, participation involves in-person attendance in Switzerland. Candidates should consider their ability to attend the required sessions and workshops.

Finally, applicants should not assume that the travel assistance represents complete financial coverage. The call specifies particular limits for travel and indicates that accommodation subsidies are available only to a limited number of students.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

A competitive application should demonstrate a clear connection between the applicant’s doctoral research and the objectives of the LIVES programme.

Make the Life Course Connection Explicit

Do not assume that the selection committee will automatically see the connection.

Explain precisely how the thesis examines:

  • Change over time
  • Life transitions
  • Trajectories
  • Turning points
  • Accumulation or depletion
  • Age and ageing
  • Intergenerational processes
  • Longitudinal patterns
  • Policy implications across the life span

Strengthen the Motivation Letter

The cover letter should go beyond saying that the programme is prestigious or interesting.

Explain specifically why LIVES is relevant to the doctoral project and identify the theoretical or methodological skills you hope to develop.

Prepare the Supervisor Early

Because a supervisor support letter is required, applicants should approach their supervisor well before the deadline.

Waiting until the final days could create unnecessary delays.

Make the 500-Word Abstract Count

The abstract has a maximum of approximately 500 words, so every paragraph should have a purpose.

A strong abstract should quickly establish the research problem, research question, theoretical perspective, methodology and expected contribution.

Demonstrate Methodological Interest

Because the programme includes several methodological workshops, applicants should explain how longitudinal or life course methods could strengthen their research.

Contact Information

Applicants who need clarification can contact the LIVES Doctoral Programme.

Programme Officer: Dr. Charikleia Lampraki

Email: doctoral-centre-lives@unige.ch

The Centre LIVES can also be contacted through:

Telephone: +41 21 692 38 71

General email: lives@unil.ch

Programme Locations

The programme operates across two Swiss academic locations.

Lausanne

LIVES – Swiss Centre of Expertise in Life Course Research

Bâtiment Géopolis
1015 Lausanne
5th Floor
Switzerland

Geneva

CIGEV, University of Geneva

22 chemin de Pinchat
1227 Carouge
Switzerland

Application Link

Interested doctoral candidates should use the official LIVES application page to submit their application and supporting documents.

Official application page: HERE

Additional information about the 2026–27 programme, including workshops and events, is available through the LIVES programme outline.

More PHD programs available on the OFY Website HERE

Conclusion

The LIVES Doctoral Programme 2026–2029 is a valuable academic development opportunity for early-stage PhD researchers whose work examines people’s lives, trajectories and transitions over time.

Through theoretical training, methodological workshops, doctoral presentations, individual expert feedback and an international peer network, the programme offers participants an opportunity to strengthen both the conceptual and practical dimensions of their doctoral research.

The opportunity is particularly relevant to researchers working in sociology, demography, psychology, epidemiology, economics, political science, neuroscience, history, gender studies, health sciences and related disciplines, provided that their doctoral research incorporates a meaningful life course or lifespan perspective.

Applicants should remember that they must already be affiliated with an academic institution, have appropriate funding for their PhD, meet the English-language requirement and be able to participate in the programme’s in-person activities.

Most importantly, prospective applicants should begin preparing their supporting documents early, especially the supervisor recommendation and official academic affiliation document.

Application deadline: 30 September 2026.

For eligible doctoral researchers interested in life course research, longitudinal methods and interdisciplinary academic development, the LIVES Doctoral Programme represents an opportunity to become part of an established international research community while gaining specialised training that can strengthen their PhD journey and future academic career.

item.content:encoded:
The European Union provides extensive funding opportunities for research, innovation, healthcare, climate action, regional development, sustainability, and economic growth through a range of major programmes managed or supported by the European Commission.

Among these programmes, Horizon Europe stands out as the European Union’s principal research and innovation programme for the 2021–2027 period, with a substantial budget of €95.5 billion. The programme is designed to support cutting-edge research and innovation, strengthen European competitiveness, address global challenges, contribute to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, and help develop technologies and knowledge capable of creating long-term social and economic impact.

However, Horizon Europe is only one component of the wider European funding landscape. The European Commission also highlights programmes covering healthcare, climate change, biodiversity, clean energy, regional development, economic and social cohesion, technical reforms, agriculture, maritime development, and research in strategic industrial sectors such as coal and steel.

This makes the European Commission’s research and innovation funding ecosystem particularly relevant to universities, researchers, research organizations, businesses, public institutions, innovators, and organizations working on major societal and economic challenges.

What Is Horizon Europe?

Horizon Europe is the European Union’s research and innovation programme for the period 2021–2027.

With a total budget of €95.5 billion, it represents one of the world’s major public funding frameworks for research and innovation.

The programme is designed to support projects that can contribute to:

  • Scientific excellence
  • Technological development
  • Innovation
  • Economic growth
  • Industrial competitiveness
  • Climate action
  • Sustainable development
  • Policy development
  • International collaboration
  • Job creation
  • Knowledge creation
  • Technological advancement

Horizon Europe also seeks to strengthen the European Research Area by supporting collaboration among researchers, institutions, businesses, policymakers, and other stakeholders.

Key Objectives of Horizon Europe

The Horizon Europe programme has been established to address both European and global challenges through research and innovation.

Its broad objectives include:

1. Tackling Climate Change

Research and innovation supported through Horizon Europe can contribute to Europe’s climate objectives and broader global efforts to address climate change.

Projects can help develop new technologies, processes, policies, and approaches capable of reducing environmental impacts and supporting climate resilience.

2. Supporting the UN Sustainable Development Goals

Horizon Europe contributes to efforts aimed at achieving the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

Research and innovation can help address interconnected challenges involving:

  • Poverty
  • Health
  • Education
  • Energy
  • Climate
  • Food systems
  • Industry
  • Infrastructure
  • Sustainable cities
  • Environmental protection
  • Economic development

3. Strengthening European Competitiveness

Innovation is considered an important driver of economic growth.

Horizon Europe therefore supports the development and dissemination of knowledge and technologies that can strengthen Europe’s industrial competitiveness.

4. Creating Jobs and Economic Growth

Research and innovation can create new industries, products, services, technologies, and employment opportunities.

The programme seeks to maximize the economic and societal impact of research investments.

5. Strengthening International Collaboration

Horizon Europe facilitates collaboration between researchers, institutions, organizations, and other stakeholders.

This collaborative approach can help researchers combine expertise, infrastructure, data, and resources to address complex challenges.

Why EU Research and Innovation Funding Matters

Research and innovation are central to addressing challenges that cannot be solved through isolated actions.

Issues such as climate change, public health, energy security, industrial transformation, environmental degradation, and sustainable development require long-term investment in knowledge and technology.

European Union funding programmes help support this work by providing financial resources for research, innovation, infrastructure, collaboration, and implementation.

For researchers and organizations, these programmes can provide opportunities to transform research ideas into:

  • New technologies
  • Scientific discoveries
  • Innovative products
  • Policy recommendations
  • Demonstration projects
  • Sustainable solutions
  • New businesses
  • Improved public service

 

Apply here

Other European Commission Funding Programmes

The European Commission’s research and innovation funding landscape extends beyond Horizon Europe.

The information provided highlights several additional programmes.

These include:

  1. EU4Health
  2. Cohesion Fund
  3. LIFE Programme
  4. European Regional Development Fund
  5. Technical Support Instrument
  6. European Structural and Investment Funds
  7. Research Fund for Coal and Steel

Each programme has a different purpose, target group, funding structure, and eligibility framework.

Visit here for more details on Horizon Europe and EU Research Funding 2026

EU4Health Programme

The EU4Health programme is the European Union’s fourth and largest health programme since the EU health programmes began in 2003.

It has a budget of €5.3 billion.

The programme is implemented by the European Health and Digital Executive Agency (HaDEA).

EU4Health is designed to strengthen Europe’s health systems and contribute to improved preparedness and resilience.

The programme is particularly relevant to organizations and stakeholders working on health-related challenges and European health priorities.

Why EU4Health Is Important

Healthcare systems face increasingly complex challenges, including emerging health threats, cross-border health issues, and the need for stronger preparedness.

A large-scale EU health programme can support initiatives that contribute to:

  • Health system resilience
  • Public health
  • Health preparedness
  • European health cooperation
  • Health-related innovation
  • Capacity building

Specific eligibility and funding conditions depend on individual EU4Health calls.

Cohesion Fund

The Cohesion Fund is another major European Union funding instrument.

It is specifically aimed at EU countries whose gross national income (GNI) per inhabitant is less than 90% of the EU average.

Its overarching objective is to help reduce economic and social disparities between regions and countries within the European Union.

The fund also supports sustainable development.

Its priorities can therefore contribute to strengthening economic and social cohesion while encouraging environmentally sustainable development.

LIFE Programme: Climate, Nature and Clean Energy Funding

The LIFE Programme 2021–2027 is another important European Union funding programme highlighted on the European Commission’s research and innovation funding page.

The programme is divided into four major sub-programmes:

Nature and Biodiversity

This area focuses on protecting biodiversity and supporting nature conservation.

Potential areas include:

  • Biodiversity protection
  • Ecosystem conservation
  • Nature restoration
  • Environmental management

Circular Economy and Quality of Life

This component addresses environmental challenges associated with resource use, pollution, waste, and sustainable production and consumption.

Climate Change Mitigation and Adaptation

This area supports efforts to:

  • Reduce greenhouse gas emissions
  • Address climate change
  • Improve climate resilience
  • Develop adaptation strategies
  • Support climate-related innovation

Clean Energy Transition

The clean energy component supports the transition toward more sustainable energy systems.

This can include initiatives designed to improve energy efficiency and accelerate the adoption of clean energy solutions.

European Regional Development Fund

The European Regional Development Fund (ERDF) aims to strengthen economic and social cohesion within the European Union.

A major purpose of the fund is to help correct economic and regional imbalances.

The ERDF focuses investment on priority areas that can contribute to regional development.

One of its important areas is:

Research and innovation.

This makes the ERDF particularly relevant to regional initiatives seeking to strengthen innovation ecosystems, economic development, infrastructure, and research capabilities.

Technical Support Instrument

The Technical Support Instrument provides tailor-made technical expertise to EU countries undertaking reforms.

Rather than functioning solely as conventional project funding, the instrument provides technical assistance designed around specific reform needs.

This can help participating countries:

  • Design reforms
  • Implement reforms
  • Strengthen administrative capacity
  • Improve institutional performance
  • Develop technical solutions
  • Address complex policy challenges

The programme is particularly relevant to public authorities working on structural and institutional reforms.

European Structural and Investment Funds

The European Structural and Investment Funds (ESIF) represent another major component of European Union funding.

According to the information provided, more than half of EU funding is channelled through the five European Structural and Investment Funds.

These funds are jointly managed by:

  • The European Commission
  • European Union Member States

Their broad purpose is to support:

  • Job creation
  • Sustainable economic development
  • Social development
  • Environmental sustainability
  • Regional development

Five European Structural and Investment Funds

The five funds cover different areas of European development.

They include:

1. European Regional Development Fund

Supports regional economic and social development, including research and innovation.

2. European Social Fund

Supports employment, skills, education, training, and social inclusion.

3. Cohesion Fund

Supports EU countries meeting the relevant income criterion and contributes to economic and social cohesion.

4. European Agricultural Fund for Rural Development

Supports rural development and agricultural priorities.

5. European Maritime and Fisheries Fund

Supports areas associated with maritime activities, fisheries, and related development priorities.

The eligibility and funding mechanisms differ among the individual funds.

Research Fund for Coal and Steel

The Research Fund for Coal and Steel (RFCS) supports research projects related to the coal and steel sectors.

The fund provides support to organizations including:

  • Universities
  • Research centres
  • Private companies

According to the information provided, approximately €55 million is made available annually for research in these sectors, with the historical reference noting €47.7 million for 2015.

The RFCS provides a mechanism for supporting research and technological development in sectors undergoing significant industrial transformation.

Who Can Benefit From European Research and Innovation Funding?

Because the page covers multiple funding programmes rather than a single grant competition, the potential beneficiaries vary considerably.

Depending on the programme and specific call, funding opportunities may be relevant to:

  • Universities
  • Academic researchers
  • Research centres
  • Scientific institutions
  • Private companies
  • Innovative businesses
  • Public authorities
  • Regional organizations
  • Non-governmental organizations where eligible
  • Healthcare organizations
  • Environmental organizations
  • Agricultural organizations
  • Industrial stakeholders
  • Technology developers
  • International research partnerships

However, applicants should not assume that an organization automatically qualifies simply because it belongs to one of these categories.

Eligibility must always be checked against the specific funding call.

What Types of Projects Can EU Funding Support?

The broad funding ecosystem described on the European Commission page covers an extensive range of activities.

Depending on the programme, projects can address areas such as:

  • Scientific research
  • Technological innovation
  • Climate change
  • Environmental protection
  • Biodiversity
  • Healthcare
  • Clean energy
  • Circular economy
  • Regional development
  • Sustainable agriculture
  • Rural development
  • Maritime development
  • Industrial research
  • Coal and steel research
  • Economic development
  • Social development
  • Institutional reform

This breadth makes EU funding particularly significant for organizations working on complex multidisciplinary challenges.

Horizon Europe and International Collaboration

One of the central strengths of Horizon Europe is its emphasis on collaboration.

Modern research challenges often require expertise from multiple disciplines and institutions.

For example, a climate project might require collaboration among:

  • Climate scientists
  • Economists
  • Engineers
  • Policymakers
  • Technology companies
  • Environmental organizations
  • Data scientists

Similarly, a healthcare innovation project might require cooperation among:

  • Medical researchers
  • Universities
  • Hospitals
  • Technology developers
  • Public authorities
  • Health organizations

Horizon Europe’s collaborative structure is designed to facilitate such partnerships and maximize the impact of research and innovation.

Contribution to the European Research Area

Horizon Europe also contributes to strengthening the European Research Area (ERA).

The European Research Area seeks to create stronger cooperation and coordination across European research systems.

By supporting collaboration and knowledge sharing, EU research funding can help:

  • Connect researchers
  • Improve research capacity
  • Share scientific knowledge
  • Encourage innovation
  • Strengthen institutions
  • Improve the impact of research investments

Is There a Deadline for This Opportunity?

No specific application deadline is stated in the information provided.

This is important because the page is a general overview of EU funding programmes and does not represent one individual grant call.

Different programmes and individual calls have different:

  • Opening dates
  • Submission deadlines
  • Eligibility rules
  • Funding amounts
  • Application procedures
  • Consortium requirements

Applicants should therefore identify the specific programme and call relevant to their project before preparing an application.

How to Find an Appropriate EU Funding Opportunity

Researchers and organizations interested in EU funding should begin by identifying the nature of their project.

Step 1: Define the Project

Clearly establish:

  • The problem being addressed
  • Research objectives
  • Expected outcomes
  • Target beneficiaries
  • Proposed methodology
  • Innovation component
  • Expected impact

Step 2: Identify the Appropriate Programme

A climate project may be more relevant to LIFE or a suitable Horizon Europe call, while a health-focused initiative could be relevant to EU4Health.

Regional infrastructure or innovation projects may fall under ERDF or related funding instruments.

Step 3: Check Eligibility

Review the specific call carefully.

Important eligibility considerations can include:

  • Applicant type
  • Country eligibility
  • Consortium requirements
  • Research area
  • Project duration
  • Funding limits
  • Co-financing requirements
  • Partnership requirements

Step 4: Review the Deadline

Every individual call has its own submission deadline.

Applicants should never rely on the general programme period as an application deadline.

Step 5: Prepare the Proposal

A competitive EU proposal generally needs to clearly demonstrate:

  • Excellence
  • Relevance
  • Innovation
  • Feasibility
  • Impact
  • Appropriate implementation
  • Strong partnership arrangements where required

Key Difference Between Horizon Europe and Other EU Funds

Although all of these programmes form part of the broader European funding ecosystem, they serve different purposes.

For example:

Programme Main Focus
Horizon Europe Research and innovation
EU4Health Health
LIFE Environment, climate and clean energy
ERDF Regional development and cohesion
Cohesion Fund Economic and social cohesion
Technical Support Instrument Reform support and technical expertise
ESIF Regional, social, agricultural and maritime development
RFCS Coal and steel research

This distinction is important when searching for funding because selecting an inappropriate programme can result in an application that does not align with the fund’s objectives.

Why Researchers and Innovators Should Explore EU Funding

European Union research and innovation programmes provide access to some of the world’s largest public funding mechanisms for research, development, sustainability, and innovation.

For eligible organizations, successful funding can provide resources to:

  • Conduct research
  • Develop new technologies
  • Test innovative solutions
  • Build partnerships
  • Address societal challenges
  • Expand research capacity
  • Strengthen institutions
  • Create economic opportunities
  • Support environmental sustainability
  • Contribute to international policy objectives

For researchers and organizations working on ambitious projects, EU funding can therefore provide an important route for moving ideas from research and development toward real-world implementation.

Important Considerations Before Applying

Potential applicants should remember that the information on this page is a programme overview, not a single funding application announcement.

Before applying, applicants should carefully confirm:

  1. Whether their country is eligible.
  2. Whether their organization is an eligible applicant.
  3. Whether their project matches the specific call.
  4. Whether partnerships are required.
  5. Whether international partners are permitted.
  6. Whether co-financing is required.
  7. What expenses are eligible.
  8. The maximum available funding.
  9. The project duration.
  10. The exact application deadline.
  11. Required supporting documents.
  12. Evaluation criteria.

These details can differ substantially between EU funding programmes and individual calls.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Horizon Europe?

Horizon Europe is the European Union’s main research and innovation programme for 2021–2027, with a budget of €95.5 billion.

What does Horizon Europe fund?

It supports research and innovation aimed at addressing global challenges, strengthening European competitiveness, supporting sustainable development, and creating and spreading excellent knowledge and technologies.

Is Horizon Europe a scholarship?

No. Horizon Europe is primarily a research and innovation funding programme, supporting projects and organizations rather than functioning as a conventional student scholarship.

Is there one application deadline for Horizon Europe?

No. Horizon Europe consists of numerous calls, each with its own eligibility requirements and deadlines.

Can individuals apply?

Eligibility depends on the specific call. Many EU research and innovation opportunities are structured around organizations, research institutions, companies, or collaborative consortia.

Can organizations outside Europe participate?

International participation can be possible in specific Horizon Europe calls, but eligibility varies. Applicants should check the individual call conditions rather than assuming worldwide eligibility.

What is the EU4Health programme?

EU4Health is the European Union’s fourth and largest health programme since the launch of EU health programmes in 2003. It has a budget of €5.3 billion.

What is the LIFE Programme?

LIFE is an EU programme covering nature and biodiversity, circular economy and quality of life, climate change mitigation and adaptation, and clean energy transition.

What is the Research Fund for Coal and Steel?

RFCS supports research projects in the coal and steel sectors and can provide funding to universities, research centres, and private companies.

Are all the programmes open to the same applicants?

No. Each funding programme and individual call has its own eligibility conditions.

Conclusion

The European Commission’s research and innovation funding ecosystem provides a broad range of opportunities for organizations working across research, technology, climate action, healthcare, environmental protection, regional development, sustainable energy, agriculture, and industrial innovation.

At the centre of this ecosystem is Horizon Europe, the EU’s €95.5 billion research and innovation programme for 2021–2027. Through Horizon Europe, the European Union seeks to support excellent research, technological development, international collaboration, climate action, the Sustainable Development Goals, economic growth, job creation, and European competitiveness.

Beyond Horizon Europe, programmes such as EU4Health, LIFE, the European Regional Development Fund, the Cohesion Fund, the Technical Support Instrument, the European Structural and Investment Funds, and the Research Fund for Coal and Steel address additional priorities across health, climate, environment, regional development, economic cohesion, reform, agriculture, maritime activities, and industrial research.

For researchers, universities, businesses, public institutions, and other eligible organizations, these programmes can provide important opportunities to secure funding for ambitious projects and turn innovative ideas into measurable social, environmental, scientific, and economic impact.

However, there is no single deadline or universal eligibility requirement for all the programmes described on the page. Applicants must identify the specific funding call relevant to their project and carefully review its eligibility criteria, funding rules, partnership requirements, application procedure, and submission deadline before applying.

For more global grant opportunities visit here

item.content:encoded:
The African Development Bank (AfDB) is inviting applications for a Junior Consultant to support the Independent Development Evaluation (IDEV) function in Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire. The consultancy offers an opportunity for an early-career professional to contribute to knowledge management, communication, evaluation capacity development and knowledge-sharing activities within the Bank.

The consultant will support IDEV3 in implementing its work programme and contribute to activities that strengthen the use and dissemination of evaluation knowledge across the African Development Bank and its Regional Member Countries.

About the Junior Consultant Opportunity

The selected Junior Consultant will provide support across several areas, including knowledge management, communication, evaluation capacity development and the organization of knowledge-sharing events.

The role combines technical, administrative and logistical responsibilities, making it suitable for candidates interested in development evaluation, knowledge management, communications and international development.

The consultant will work with IDEV3 to support the implementation of its planned activities and contribute to the preparation and dissemination of knowledge and communication products.

Key Responsibilities

The Junior Consultant will be expected to support IDEV3 in areas such as:

  • Providing technical, administrative and logistical support for events and other activities.
  • Supporting the organization of knowledge-sharing events.
  • Contributing to the preparation of IDEV knowledge products.
  • Supporting quality assurance of communication and knowledge materials.
  • Assisting with the translation and dissemination of IDEV products.
  • Supporting evaluation capacity development initiatives.
  • Contributing to initiatives within the African Development Bank and its Regional Member Countries.
  • Supporting knowledge management and communication activities related to IDEV’s work programme.

Areas of Work

The consultancy focuses particularly on four key areas:

Knowledge Management

The consultant will support activities aimed at organizing, managing and sharing knowledge generated through development evaluation work.

Communication

The role involves contributing to the preparation, quality assurance, translation and dissemination of IDEV’s communication and knowledge products.

Evaluation Capacity Development

The consultant will support initiatives designed to strengthen evaluation capacity within the African Development Bank and across its Regional Member Countries.

Knowledge-Sharing Events

The consultant will provide technical, administrative and logistical support for events and activities designed to facilitate knowledge exchange.

Consultant Details

Position: Junior Consultant
Organization: African Development Bank
Department/Unit: Independent Development Evaluation (IDEV)
Location: Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire
Consultant Type: Junior Consultant
Job Family: Other
Publication Date: 13 August 2026
Application Deadline: 24 August 2026

Who Should Consider Applying?

This opportunity may be particularly relevant to early-career professionals interested in development evaluation, knowledge management, communications, research, international development and capacity development.

Candidates should carefully review the official vacancy announcement for the complete eligibility criteria, qualifications, experience requirements and application instructions before submitting an application.

Why Consider This Opportunity?

Working with the African Development Bank provides an opportunity to gain experience in a major African development institution while contributing to activities related to evaluation, knowledge sharing and institutional learning.

The consultancy can also provide valuable exposure to how development knowledge is prepared, communicated and used to support decision-making within the Bank and its Regional Member Countries.

For candidates seeking to build a career in international development, evaluation, communications or knowledge management, this role offers an opportunity to work within a professional development-focused environment.

How to Apply

Interested candidates should review the official African Development Bank vacancy announcement and follow the application instructions provided by the Bank.

Application Deadline: 24 August 2026

Applicants should ensure that their application is submitted before the closing date and that all required information and supporting documents are provided.

Official African Development Bank Careers:
African Development Bank Current Vacancies

Important Note

The position is based in Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire, and applicants should carefully review the official vacancy announcement for detailed requirements before applying.

The vacancy was published on 13 August 2026 and closes on 24 August 2026, giving interested candidates a limited period to prepare and submit their applications.

Conclusion

The African Development Bank Junior Consultant opportunity offers an opportunity for an early-career professional to contribute to knowledge management, communication, evaluation capacity development and knowledge-sharing activities within the Bank’s Independent Development Evaluation function.

If you have an interest in development evaluation, knowledge management, communication or international development, this consultancy in Abidjan could provide valuable professional exposure and experience.

Application Deadline: 24 August 2026

item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Department of the Treasury International Affairs Junior Fellowship is now recruiting for its 2027–2029 cohort, offering a highly selective two-year opportunity for recent college graduates who want to contribute to international economic and financial policy in the United States.

The Junior Fellowship places talented early-career professionals in the Treasury’s Office of International Affairs (IA), where they can gain direct exposure to international economic policy, financial developments, multilateral institutions, and high-level engagement with governments and international organizations.

For graduates interested in international economics, public policy, finance, international relations, global development, financial diplomacy, or U.S. economic policy, this program offers an opportunity to begin a career at the center of U.S. international economic affairs.

Junior Fellows may work on policy proposals, analyze international economic and financial developments, conduct analytical studies, and support senior Treasury officials participating in bilateral and multilateral meetings involving institutions and forums such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF), World Bank, G7, and G20.

The program is designed as a fixed two-year appointment, giving fellows an opportunity to develop specialized knowledge, professional experience, and a deeper understanding of how the U.S. government approaches international economic and financial issues.

About the International Affairs Junior Fellowship

The International Affairs Junior Fellowship is a highly selective early-career program within the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of International Affairs.

It is designed specifically for new college graduates who want to work on issues affecting the international economy and the United States’ relationships with foreign governments and international financial institutions.

During the two-year program, Junior Fellows can be exposed to multiple policy areas rather than being restricted to a single narrow subject.

This allows participants to develop a broad understanding of:

  • International economic policy
  • Global financial developments
  • International financial institutions
  • Economic diplomacy
  • Financial policy
  • International trade
  • Foreign exchange
  • Export credits
  • Regional economic relationships
  • Multilateral cooperation
  • U.S. engagement with international institutions

The program can therefore provide a strong foundation for individuals considering long-term careers in government, international organizations, finance, policy research, consulting, academia, or related fields.

What Junior Fellows Do

Junior Fellows perform a variety of analytical, policy, and program-support responsibilities.

Their work may include:

  • Developing policy proposals
  • Analyzing international economic developments
  • Monitoring international financial developments
  • Conducting analytical studies
  • Supporting policy research
  • Preparing materials for senior officials
  • Supporting bilateral meetings
  • Supporting multilateral meetings
  • Participating in international policy discussions
  • Developing knowledge of international economic and financial issues

The fellowship is intended to provide meaningful exposure to the work of Treasury’s Office of International Affairs rather than functioning simply as an observational placement.

Exposure to International Economic Policy

One of the most distinctive features of the program is the opportunity to work on issues affecting the international economic system.

Junior Fellows may gain insight into how the U.S. government approaches economic relationships with countries and regions around the world.

They can also develop an understanding of how international economic developments influence:

  • U.S. economic policy
  • Financial stability
  • International trade
  • Currency and foreign exchange issues
  • Development finance
  • Global economic cooperation
  • International financial institutions

This makes the program particularly relevant for graduates who want to understand the intersection of economics, diplomacy, finance, and government.

Opportunities to Support IMF, World Bank, G7 and G20 Engagement

Junior Fellows support bilateral and multilateral meetings involving senior Treasury officials and international counterparts.

This can include engagement connected to major international institutions and forums such as:

  • International Monetary Fund
  • World Bank
  • G7
  • G20

Junior Fellows often participate in these meetings and may have opportunities to travel abroad.

This exposure can provide valuable insight into how international economic policy is discussed and coordinated among governments and global institutions.

Regional and Functional Office Placements

Junior Fellows will be placed in either a regional office or a functional office within Treasury’s Office of International Affairs.

Regional Offices

Regional offices oversee Treasury’s engagement with counterpart finance ministries and treasuries around the world.

Working in a regional office can provide fellows with exposure to the economic and financial relationships between the United States and specific countries or regions.

Potential areas of learning include:

  • Regional economic developments
  • Bilateral economic relationships
  • International financial policy
  • Engagement with foreign finance ministries
  • Economic and financial analysis
  • Regional policy challenges

Functional Offices

Functional offices oversee Treasury’s engagement with international financial institutions and help structure broader Treasury policy.

Functional policy areas can include:

  • International trade
  • Export credits
  • Foreign exchange
  • International financial institutions
  • Broader international economic policy

The distinction between regional and functional offices allows fellows to develop expertise either around particular geographic relationships or around specialized international economic policy areas.

Who Is the Fellowship Designed For?

The program is intended for new college graduates and individuals who have recently completed, or are about to complete, their undergraduate education.

Strong candidates will generally have a bachelor’s degree with relevant academic preparation in areas such as:

  • Economics
  • Public policy
  • Finance
  • International relations
  • Related disciplines

The announcement specifically states that, because of the structure of the program, preference is given to undergraduates.

Applicants should therefore demonstrate a strong academic interest in international economic policy and related subjects.

Educational Qualifications

A bachelor’s degree is the central academic qualification identified in the announcement.

Relevant coursework may include subjects such as:

  • Microeconomics
  • Macroeconomics
  • International economics
  • Public finance
  • Financial markets
  • International relations
  • Public policy
  • International development
  • Political economy
  • Statistics
  • Quantitative analysis

Although the announcement does not provide a specific list of required courses, candidates should be able to demonstrate academic preparation relevant to the duties performed by International Affairs Junior Fellows.

Required Work and Extracurricular Experience

In addition to academic qualifications, applicants must demonstrate 52 weeks, or 2,080 hours, of relevant experience.

Importantly, the required experience does not have to come exclusively from traditional full-time employment.

The announcement allows relevant experience to include:

  • Paid employment
  • Unpaid work
  • Volunteer activities
  • Extracurricular activities
  • Work-study experiences
  • Other relevant professional or academic activities

Applicants should carefully document this experience in their resumes.

For each activity, candidates are encouraged to clearly describe:

  • Position or role
  • Responsibilities
  • Duties performed
  • Start date
  • End date
  • Number of hours worked per week
  • Relevance to the fellowship

For example, candidates should provide specific dates and weekly hours rather than simply listing an organization or job title.

Resume Requirements

The resume submitted for the application must not exceed two pages.

This is particularly important because candidates are expected to demonstrate their required 2,080 hours of relevant experience while keeping the document concise.

Applicants should therefore prioritize:

  • Relevant responsibilities
  • Analytical experience
  • Research experience
  • Policy experience
  • Economic or financial work
  • Leadership activities
  • International relations experience
  • Volunteer experience
  • Extracurricular activities relevant to the position

Rather than simply listing job titles, applicants should explain what they actually accomplished and how their responsibilities relate to the work of Treasury’s Office of International Affairs.

Application Documents

Applicants must submit the following materials:

  1. Cover letter
  2. Resume
  3. One recommendation letter
  4. Transcript or transcripts demonstrating academic qualifications and career potential

The documents should collectively demonstrate the applicant’s:

  • Academic preparation
  • Relevant experience
  • Analytical capabilities
  • Career potential
  • Interest in international economic policy
  • Suitability for the Junior Fellowship

Additional Information Required in the Application Email

The application email must also include specific information.

Applicants must:

  • Indicate their desired start date.
  • Confirm that they are U.S. citizens.
  • Confirm that they can provide documentation of U.S. citizenship.
  • Note veterans’ preference, if applicable.
  • Include a resume demonstrating the required 52 weeks or 2,080 hours of relevant experience.

These details should be included carefully because they are explicitly required as part of the application process.

National Security Clearance Requirement

Candidates must be able to obtain and maintain a national security clearance.

This is an important condition of the fellowship because the position is within the U.S. Department of the Treasury and involves work related to government international affairs.

Applicants should therefore understand that meeting the academic and experience requirements alone does not guarantee appointment.

The ability to obtain and maintain the required security clearance is also necessary.

U.S. Citizenship Requirement

U.S. citizenship is specifically required.

Applicants must confirm in their application that they are U.S. citizens and must be able to provide documentation proving their citizenship.

Therefore, this opportunity should not be treated as an open international fellowship for applicants from all countries.

Individuals who are not U.S. citizens do not meet the stated citizenship requirement.

Veterans’ Preference

Applicants are asked to identify veterans’ preference, if applicable, when submitting their application.

Candidates who qualify for veterans’ preference should make sure that this information is clearly stated in their application email.

Selection and Screening Process

The Junior Fellowship is highly selective.

Applications will initially undergo a screening process.

Candidates who pass the first round of screening will be asked to respond to two short essay questions.

These additional questions provide candidates with another opportunity to demonstrate:

  • Analytical thinking
  • Written communication
  • Policy interests
  • Motivation
  • Understanding of international affairs
  • Career objectives

Applicants should be prepared to provide clear, well-structured, and thoughtful responses if they advance to this stage.

Application Evaluation Timeline

Applications will be evaluated in December 2026.

Successful candidates are expected to begin their fellowship in summer 2027, although an alternative start date may be mutually agreed upon.

The program is scheduled as a fixed two-year appointment, covering the 2027–2029 period.

Fellowship Level and Compensation

Junior Fellows are usually hired at the GS-9 level.

They also receive standard U.S. Department of the Treasury benefits.

The GS-9 classification places the position within the U.S. federal government employment structure and reflects the professional nature of the fellowship.

What Happens After the Fellowship?

The Junior Fellowship can serve as a launching point for a wide variety of professional and academic pathways.

According to the program information, previous fellows have gone on to pursue opportunities including:

  • Employment at the U.S. Department of the Treasury
  • Other U.S. government employment
  • Private-sector careers
  • Graduate education
  • Law school
  • Public policy programs
  • International relations programs
  • Finance and business graduate studies

This range of outcomes demonstrates the versatility of the experience gained through the program.

Career Development Opportunities

During the fellowship, participants can develop skills that are valuable across government, business, academia, and international organizations.

These may include:

  • Economic analysis
  • Financial analysis
  • Policy research
  • Policy writing
  • International affairs analysis
  • Government engagement
  • Professional communication
  • Meeting support
  • Strategic thinking
  • Research methodology
  • Cross-cultural communication
  • Multilateral policy engagement

The experience can therefore provide a strong foundation for long-term careers in international economic affairs.

Information Sessions for Applicants

The Junior Fellows recruiting committee plans to host three information sessions before the application deadline.

These sessions will be led by current fellows from various International Affairs offices.

Participants will have the opportunity to:

  • Ask questions about the Junior Fellowship
  • Learn about the application process
  • Hear directly from current fellows
  • Understand what it is like to work in Treasury’s Office of International Affairs
  • Learn about different International Affairs offices
  • Gain insight into the fellowship experience

The announcement states that dates and registration information will be published on the relevant page in late summer 2026.

Applicants should monitor the Treasury careers information for updates.

Application Deadline

The deadline to apply for the International Affairs Junior Fellowship 2027–2029 is:

October 31, 2026

Applicants should submit their complete application materials by this date.

Because the program requires several documents, including a cover letter, resume, recommendation letter, and transcript or transcripts, candidates should begin preparing their application well before the deadline.

How to Apply

Applicants should submit their application materials by email to:

IAFellows@treasury.gov

The application should include:

  1. Cover letter
  2. Resume of no more than two pages
  3. One recommendation letter
  4. Transcript or transcripts
  5. Desired start date
  6. Confirmation of U.S. citizenship
  7. Veterans’ preference information, if applicable
  8. Evidence of the required 2,080 hours of relevant experience

Candidates should carefully review their documents before submission to ensure that all required information is included.

Apply here

Application Preparation Tips

Because this is a highly selective program, candidates should approach the application strategically.

1. Tailor the Resume

Do not submit a generic resume.

Emphasize experiences connected to:

  • Economics
  • Finance
  • Public policy
  • International affairs
  • Government
  • Research
  • Analysis
  • Leadership

2. Document the 2,080 Hours Clearly

Applicants should make it easy for reviewers to verify their relevant experience.

Include:

  • Dates
  • Hours per week
  • Position
  • Organization
  • Specific responsibilities

3. Keep the Resume Within Two Pages

The two-page limit means candidates should prioritize the most relevant experiences and provide specific descriptions without unnecessary information.

4. Demonstrate Analytical Skills

International Affairs work requires the ability to understand complex economic and financial developments.

Candidates should highlight experiences involving:

  • Research
  • Data analysis
  • Policy analysis
  • Writing
  • Problem-solving
  • Economic analysis

5. Prepare for the Essay Stage

Candidates who pass initial screening will receive two short essay questions.

Applicants should be prepared to communicate their ideas clearly and concisely.

6. Prepare Documentation of Citizenship

Because U.S. citizenship is a mandatory requirement, eligible candidates should be prepared to provide the necessary documentation.

For more information on this fellowship visit here

Why This Fellowship Is a Significant Opportunity

The U.S. Treasury International Affairs Junior Fellowship provides a rare opportunity for recent graduates to work directly within a major U.S. government department while gaining exposure to international economic and financial policymaking.

The fellowship combines:

  • Federal government experience
  • International economic policy
  • Financial analysis
  • Global institutions
  • Multilateral engagement
  • Professional development
  • Potential international travel
  • Graduate study preparation
  • Long-term career opportunities

For graduates interested in the relationship between economics and international affairs, this combination can provide an especially valuable early-career foundation.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the International Affairs Junior Fellowship?

It is a highly selective, fixed two-year program within the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of International Affairs for new college graduates interested in international economic policy.

When is the application deadline?

The application deadline is October 31, 2026.

When will selected fellows begin?

Applications will be evaluated in December 2026, with fellows expected to begin in summer 2027, or at another mutually agreed time.

How long does the fellowship last?

The program is a fixed two-year fellowship covering the 2027–2029 period.

What degree is required?

Strong candidates will have recently received, or will soon receive, a bachelor’s degree with relevant coursework in economics, public policy, finance, international relations, or related fields.

Is U.S. citizenship required?

Yes. Applicants must confirm that they are U.S. citizens and must be able to provide documentation.

Is professional experience required?

Applicants must demonstrate 52 weeks or 2,080 hours of relevant paid or unpaid work, volunteer, or extracurricular experience.

Can volunteer work count?

Yes. The announcement specifically allows relevant volunteer and extracurricular experience to count toward the required experience.

Can fellows travel internationally?

Junior Fellows often participate in international meetings and may have opportunities to travel abroad.

Is there a security clearance requirement?

Yes. Candidates must be able to obtain and maintain a national security clearance.

How many pages can the resume be?

The resume should not exceed two pages.

Is there an age limit?

No specific age limit is stated in the provided announcement. The program is designed for new college graduates.

Can international applicants apply?

The program requires U.S. citizenship. Therefore, applicants who do not hold U.S. citizenship do not meet the stated eligibility requirement.

Conclusion

The U.S. Department of the Treasury International Affairs Junior Fellowship 2027–2029 offers an exceptional early-career pathway for qualified U.S. citizens who want to work at the intersection of international economics, finance, public policy, and global affairs. Through this highly selective two-year program, Junior Fellows can contribute to policy development, analyze international economic and financial developments, support senior Treasury officials, and gain exposure to major institutions and forums including the IMF, World Bank, G7, and G20.

With opportunities to work in regional or functional offices, participate in international meetings, potentially travel abroad, and develop valuable analytical and policy skills, the fellowship can provide a strong foundation for careers in government, the private sector, international affairs, finance, and graduate education.

Eligible recent or soon-to-be graduates should carefully prepare their cover letter, two-page resume, recommendation letter, transcripts, and required experience documentation before submitting their application to IAFellows@treasury.gov. The deadline is October 31, 2026, making early preparation particularly important for candidates seeking to join the 2027–2029 International Affairs Junior Fellowship cohort.
