item.content:encoded:
The Stockholm Water Prize 2027 is now accepting nominations for individuals, institutions, and organisations that have made exceptional and lasting contributions to humanity’s understanding, management, protection, and sustainable use of water resources.

Often regarded as one of the world’s most prestigious recognitions in the field of water, the Stockholm Water Prize celebrates achievements that have made a substantial difference to water science, water management, human well-being, ecosystems, and the sustainable development of societies.

The 2027 nomination period is currently open, giving researchers, professionals, institutions, organisations, policymakers, practitioners, and other qualified nominators an opportunity to put forward outstanding water champions whose work deserves international recognition.

The nomination period runs from 17 March 2026 to 15 September 2026.

The prize recognises contributions across a broad range of disciplines, meaning that eligible achievements do not have to come exclusively from traditional water science. Contributions may involve natural sciences, engineering, technology, education, policy, governance, management, human rights, international cooperation, sanitation, water supply, or practical implementation.

About the Stockholm Water Prize

The Stockholm Water Prize is awarded to an individual, institution, or organisation that has made a substantial scientific or other contribution to understanding water resources and to their sustainable use and protection.

The central objective of the prize is to recognise work that has contributed to improved health and well-being for people and ecosystems.

This broad mandate means the award can recognise both groundbreaking scientific discoveries and practical achievements that have transformed how water is governed, managed, supplied, protected, or understood.

The contribution of a potential laureate may therefore come from academic research, technological innovation, public policy, community-level implementation, institutional reform, education, advocacy, or other significant water-related work.

Stockholm Water Prize 2027 Nomination Period

Nominations for the 2027 Stockholm Water Prize are open during the following period:

Opening date: 17 March 2026
Deadline: 15 September 2026

Individuals and organisations wishing to nominate a candidate should submit a short nomination through the official nomination form during the nomination period.

The nomination process begins with a short submission. Candidates who are considered outstanding may subsequently be selected for a more comprehensive nomination process.

Who Can Be Nominated?

The Stockholm Water Prize is unusually broad in the types of candidates it can recognise.

A nominee may be:

  • An individual
  • An institution
  • An organisation

The nominee should have demonstrated outstanding achievements connected to water resources and should have made a meaningful contribution with lasting significance.

The work may have taken place in academia, government, industry, civil society, international organisations, communities, research institutions, or other relevant settings.

Importantly, the announcement does not establish a restriction based on nationality, country, region, race, or continent. This means that the opportunity is not presented as being limited to candidates from a particular geographic area.

Candidates from Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, Oceania, and other parts of the world can therefore potentially be considered, provided their achievements satisfy the prize requirements.

Two Major Categories of Achievement

The main achievements of the proposed laureate must fall into at least one of two major categories: Research or Policy and Practices.

1. Research

The Research category covers both basic and applied research that creates new knowledge or demonstrates scientific leadership in fields relevant to water.

This category can include researchers and research leaders whose work has significantly advanced understanding of water-related challenges.

Potential areas may include research that contributes to:

  • Understanding water resources
  • Water science
  • Sustainable water use
  • Protection of water resources
  • Water-related environmental challenges
  • Water technology
  • Scientific innovation
  • Water management
  • Ecosystem protection
  • Human health and water
  • Sustainable development
  • Other scientific fields relevant to water

The emphasis is not simply on publishing research. The nominee should have demonstrated outstanding achievement and lasting significance, together with evidence that the work has stimulated further important developments.

Scientific leadership can therefore be an important component of a strong nomination.

2. Policy and Practices

The Policy and Practices category recognises achievements that have improved the governance and management of water as a natural and economic resource, and/or as a human right and basic service.

This category is particularly broad and can include people or organisations whose practical, institutional, governmental, legal, technological, or community-based work has produced significant improvements in water management.

Relevant areas specifically include:

  • Human rights
  • Conflict resolution
  • International cooperation
  • Sustainable water-resource management
  • Safe management of water resources
  • Water supply services
  • Sanitation services
  • Development of appropriate technologies
  • Application of appropriate technologies
  • Economic principles for sustainable water management
  • Legislative approaches to water management
  • Institutional approaches to water management
  • Administrative principles for efficient water management
  • Equitable access to water
  • Sustainable provision of water services

This means the prize is not restricted to laboratory scientists or university researchers.

A policymaker, water professional, institution, technology developer, administrator, organisation, or other practitioner could potentially be recognised if their achievements have substantially improved water governance, access, sustainability, or management.

Education, Outreach and Awareness Also Matter

In addition to research and policy or practical achievements, the Stockholm Water Prize places importance on outreach and awareness raising.

For both major categories, achievements involving education, training, information dissemination, and public awareness can strengthen a candidate’s case.

This may include:

  • Educating students about water issues
  • Training water professionals
  • Building the capacity of local communities
  • Developing water-related educational programmes
  • Disseminating important water information
  • Raising awareness among decision-makers
  • Increasing public understanding of water challenges
  • Supporting community-level knowledge about water resources
  • Promoting responsible and sustainable water use

The award therefore recognises not only the creation of knowledge or implementation of solutions, but also the ability to ensure that knowledge reaches the people and institutions who can use it.

Key Eligibility Criteria

A successful nominee must demonstrate more than simply being involved in water-related work.

The Stockholm Water Prize specifically requires candidates to have made outstanding achievements of lasting significance during the last ten years.

The achievement should also have provided stimulation for further important work.

This is an important distinction for potential nominators.

Simply working in the water sector does not automatically make someone a strong candidate. A compelling nomination should demonstrate the significance, impact, originality, longevity, and wider influence of the nominee’s achievements.

A strong candidate should ideally have evidence showing that their contribution has gone beyond routine professional responsibilities and produced meaningful change or advancement.

What Makes a Strong Nomination?

The organisers emphasise that the quality of the nomination is important.

A poorly prepared nomination may fail to communicate the significance of an otherwise exceptional candidate.

A strong nomination should therefore clearly explain:

  1. Who the candidate is
  2. What the candidate has achieved
  3. Why those achievements are exceptional
  4. How the achievements relate to water
  5. Why the contribution has lasting significance
  6. What impact the work has had
  7. How the candidate’s work has stimulated further important work
  8. Which award category or categories the achievements fit into
  9. How the candidate satisfies the stated criteria
  10. What evidence supports the claims being made

The organisers encourage nominators to represent their candidate effectively rather than simply submitting incomplete information.

Support Letters May Be Required

An important requirement applies where a nomination cannot be supported by documented scientific merits.

In such circumstances, the nomination should be accompanied by at least two support letters.

The letters should come from individuals or organisations that have no direct professional or family ties to the candidate.

This requirement helps provide independent support for the nominee’s accomplishments and can strengthen the credibility of the nomination.

Nominators should therefore consider the availability of independent experts, institutions, organisations, or other credible supporters when preparing a nomination that does not have extensive documented scientific evidence.

Self-Nominations Are Not Allowed

One of the most important points for prospective candidates is that the Stockholm Water Prize does not accept self-nominations.

The official criteria explicitly state that self-nominations will be disregarded.

Therefore, individuals who believe they are suitable candidates should not attempt to nominate themselves.

Instead, they should encourage an appropriate person, institution, organisation, colleague, professional network, or other qualified nominator to submit their nomination on their behalf.

This also means that institutions and organisations should ensure that the nomination is submitted by someone other than the candidate themselves where applicable.

Who Cannot Be Nominated?

There is also a conflict-of-interest restriction.

A candidate cannot be:

  • Employed by the Stockholm Water Foundation; or
  • In a close professional relationship with the Stockholm Water Foundation or any of its associated entities.

Potential nominators should carefully consider this requirement before preparing a nomination.

How the Nomination and Selection Process Works

The Stockholm Water Prize follows a multi-stage evaluation process.

Step 1: Submit a Short Nomination

The process begins with the submission of a short nomination through the designated online nomination form.

At this stage, nominators should clearly communicate the candidate’s most important achievements and explain why the individual, institution, or organisation deserves consideration.

Step 2: Initial Selection

The Prize Committee at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences conducts an initial assessment.

The committee identifies candidates considered to have particularly outstanding achievements.

Step 3: Full Nomination

Nominators of outstanding candidates may subsequently be invited to submit a full nomination.

However, if the information provided in the initial nomination is considered sufficient for evaluation, the committee may determine that additional material is unnecessary.

Step 4: Detailed Review

The outstanding nominations are reviewed by the Prize Committee.

If the committee considers it appropriate, the nominations may also undergo peer review by external expert reviewers.

This stage allows specialists to provide additional assessment of the significance and quality of a candidate’s achievements.

Step 5: Recommendation to the Academy

Following the evaluation process, the Prize Committee presents its recommended laureate and the corresponding motivation at a General Meeting of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.

Step 6: Laureate Appointed

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences appoints the laureate at its meeting.

The Academy informs the Stockholm Water Foundation of its decision before the end of February.

Step 7: Stockholm Water Foundation Awards the Prize

The Board of the Stockholm Water Foundation then decides to award the Stockholm Water Prize in accordance with the decision made by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.

Confidentiality of Nominations

Nominators and candidates should also be aware that the nomination process is confidential.

The organisers state that nominations and all award nomination materials are confidential.

This confidentiality is important because it protects the integrity of the evaluation process and allows the relevant committees and reviewers to assess nominations appropriately.

How to Prepare a Competitive Nomination

Anyone considering nominating a water researcher, policymaker, institution, organisation, technology developer, or practitioner should approach the process strategically.

Clearly Identify the Candidate’s Greatest Achievement

Avoid filling the nomination with unnecessary background information.

Instead, identify the candidate’s most important achievements and explain why they matter.

Demonstrate Lasting Significance

Because the criteria specifically refer to achievements of lasting significance during the last ten years, the nomination should provide evidence of long-term impact.

Where possible, demonstrate how the candidate’s work has continued to influence research, policy, institutions, communities, water management, or other relevant areas.

Connect the Work to Water

A candidate may have a broad professional profile, but the nomination should clearly demonstrate how their outstanding achievements relate to water resources and their sustainable use or protection.

Demonstrate Impact

Strong nominations should move beyond statements such as “the candidate has contributed significantly.”

Instead, explain what changed because of the candidate’s work.

For example, the nomination could demonstrate improvements in:

  • Water access
  • Sanitation
  • Water quality
  • Water governance
  • Research knowledge
  • Environmental protection
  • Water-related policy
  • Institutional capacity
  • Technology
  • Community awareness
  • International cooperation
  • Conflict resolution
  • Sustainable resource management

Address the Award Criteria Directly

The organisers specifically advise nominators to compare the candidate’s qualifications with the award criteria.

A well-structured nomination should therefore make it easy for the Prize Committee to see how the candidate satisfies each requirement.

Why the Stockholm Water Prize Is Significant

Water is fundamental to human life, public health, food systems, economic development, environmental sustainability, and the survival of ecosystems.

However, water resources face increasingly complex challenges involving sustainability, pollution, scarcity, sanitation, climate pressures, governance, infrastructure, inequality, and competing demands.

Recognising individuals and organisations that successfully address these challenges can help bring greater attention to innovative approaches and encourage further work in the water sector.

The Stockholm Water Prize therefore provides an international platform for recognising achievements that contribute to better understanding and management of one of the world’s most essential resources.

Who Should Consider Making a Nomination?

The opportunity may be particularly relevant to people and organisations connected to the water sector, including:

  • Universities
  • Research institutions
  • Water professionals
  • Scientists
  • Engineers
  • Policymakers
  • Government institutions
  • International organisations
  • Non-governmental organisations
  • Environmental organisations
  • Water utilities
  • Sanitation professionals
  • Technology innovators
  • Development practitioners
  • Community organisations
  • Academic networks
  • Professional associations
  • Institutions working on water governance
  • Organisations involved in sustainable development

A nominator should focus on identifying a candidate whose achievements demonstrate the level of excellence and lasting significance expected by the prize.

Important Deadline

The nomination period for the Stockholm Water Prize 2027 closes on 15 September 2026.

Potential nominators should therefore avoid waiting until the final day.

Preparing a strong nomination may require gathering evidence, documenting achievements, identifying independent supporters where necessary, and carefully explaining how the candidate satisfies the award criteria.

How to Nominate

Nominations must be submitted through the official online nomination form designated by the organisers.

Official nomination form: Link to nomination form

The nomination period is:

17 March 2026 – 15 September 2026

More information VISIT HERE

More nomination opportunities visit OFY Website HERE

Key Details at a Glance

Detail Information
Opportunity Stockholm Water Prize 2027
Category International Award
Eligible nominee types Individual, institution, or organisation
Main areas Research; Policy and Practices
Geographic restriction None specified
Self-nomination Not permitted
Application/Nomination Online nomination form
Opening date 17 March 2026
Deadline 15 September 2026
Support letters At least two may be required where documented scientific merits are unavailable
Recent achievement requirement Outstanding achievements of lasting significance during the last 10 years
Conflict restriction Candidates employed by or closely professionally related to Stockholm Water Foundation or associated entities are ineligible
Nomination confidentiality Yes

Tips for Potential Nominators

Before submitting a nomination, consider the following:

  1. Choose the right candidate. Make sure the nominee’s achievements genuinely stand out within the water field.
  2. Focus on evidence. Explain the candidate’s achievements using concrete, verifiable information.
  3. Show lasting impact. Demonstrate why the work remains important and how it has influenced further developments.
  4. Connect achievements to the criteria. Explicitly show how the candidate fits the Research and/or Policy and Practices category.
  5. Highlight wider influence. Mention research, policy, practical implementation, education, training, outreach, or awareness-raising where relevant.
  6. Prepare independent support where necessary. If documented scientific merits are insufficient, ensure the required independent support letters are available.
  7. Complete the form carefully. The organisers specifically advise nominators to fill out all applicable fields.
  8. Keep the argument clear and concise. A strong nomination should contain enough information to establish the candidate’s excellence without burying the most important achievements in unnecessary detail.
  9. Do not submit a self-nomination. Self-nominations will be disregarded.
  10. Submit before the deadline. Ensure the nomination is completed by 15 September 2026.

Conclusion

The Stockholm Water Prize 2027 provides an opportunity to recognise exceptional individuals, institutions, and organisations whose work has made a meaningful and lasting contribution to water science, sustainable water management, water governance, human well-being, and ecosystem protection.

The award is broad enough to recognise both scientific research and practical achievements, covering areas ranging from engineering and technology to policy, human rights, sanitation, water supply, international cooperation, education, and community awareness.

A strong candidate should demonstrate outstanding achievements of lasting significance during the past ten years and evidence that their work has stimulated further important developments.

Importantly, the opportunity is not presented as being restricted to a particular country, nationality, race, or continent. Candidates from around the world can potentially be considered, provided they meet the stated criteria. However, self-nominations are not accepted, and candidates with the specified close employment or professional relationship with the Stockholm Water Foundation or its associated entities are excluded.

Anyone who knows a researcher, policymaker, water professional, institution, organisation, innovator, or practitioner whose work has made an exceptional contribution to the water sector should consider putting that candidate forward.

With the 15 September 2026 deadline approaching, nominators should begin preparing their submissions early and ensure that the nomination clearly communicates the candidate’s achievements, impact, lasting significance, and alignment with the Stockholm Water Prize criteria.

item.content:encoded:
The Civic Innovators Fellowship (CIF) 2026–2027 is inviting applications from high school students and eligible gap-year students who are passionate about making a positive difference in their communities. The fellowship is a free, virtual 16-week programme designed to equip young people with the knowledge, skills, networks and opportunities needed to become effective civic innovators.

Organized by Civics Unplugged, the fellowship brings together young people from across the United States and internationally for interactive sessions focused on history, democracy, technology, culture, leadership and purpose.

About the Civic Innovators Fellowship

The Civic Innovators Fellowship is designed for young people who are ready to take action rather than wait until the future to create change.

Over the course of the programme, Fellows participate in weekly discussion-based sessions, develop practical skills and explore how they can apply what they learn to challenges in their own communities.

Fellows also become part of a close-knit community of peers and gain opportunities to connect with alumni mentors from their region.

The programme runs across the academic year, with the fellowship beginning in September 2026 and continuing through April 2027.

Fellowship Benefits

Selected Fellows gain access to a range of learning, networking and development opportunities.

Free Virtual Programme

The Civic Innovators Fellowship is free to participate in and delivered online, making it accessible to students who meet the eligibility requirements regardless of their location.

Civic Leadership and Practical Skills

Participants develop knowledge and skills related to:

  • History and democracy
  • Technology and culture
  • Civic engagement
  • Community problem-solving
  • Leadership and personal purpose
  • Creating positive community change

Access to Funding and Opportunities

After completing the fellowship, Fellows join the Civics Unplugged Community, where they can gain access to networks and funding opportunities designed to support their civic projects and ideas.

Graduates may also receive access to paid roles, project funding and all-expenses-paid travel opportunities, as well as opportunities to connect with organizations working to create meaningful change.

Exclusive Programmes

Completion of the fellowship provides exclusive access to Civics Unplugged programmes, including Civic Innovation Academies and the Civic Innovation Lab.

Peer and Alumni Network

Fellows become part of a community of young people and alumni mentors who can provide support, connections and inspiration throughout their civic innovation journey.

Who Can Apply?

The Civic Innovators Fellowship is open to:

  • Students who are currently enrolled in high school; or
  • Students whose first gap year began in June 2026.

The programme welcomes international applicants. However, the fellowship content and additional opportunities are primarily U.S.-focused and delivered in English.

International applicants are encouraged to explain what they hope to contribute to and learn from a U.S.-focused civic programme.

No Traditional Academic Requirements

One of the distinctive features of the Civic Innovators Fellowship is its admissions philosophy.

Applicants are not required to submit GPAs, IQ tests, SAT scores, ACT scores or resumes as part of the assessment.

Instead, the programme seeks to understand applicants based on who they are, what they have done and what they hope to do.

The fellowship emphasizes potential, curiosity, commitment and a willingness to make a difference rather than relying solely on traditional academic achievements.

Fellowship Schedule

The fellowship includes required weekly live sessions.

First Fellowship Lesson: Monday, September 28, 2026

Weekly Sessions: Mondays at 7:30 PM ET

Fall Sessions End: November 16, 2026

The spring portion of the fellowship will begin in early February 2027 and conclude in early April 2027.

Applicants should only apply if they can commit to attending the required weekly live sessions.

Application Deadline

The application deadline for the Civic Innovators Fellowship 2026–2027 is:

September 4, 2026 at 11:59 PM PST

All admissions decisions are expected to be released on September 21, 2026.

Applicants who successfully submit their applications should receive a confirmation email. If a confirmation email does not arrive, applicants are advised to check their spam folder.

Application Requirements

Applicants will complete personal information questions and several short-answer questions.

The short-answer section includes questions about:

  • Personal values and identity
  • Community involvement
  • Taking initiative
  • Responsibility and leadership
  • Skills learned independently
  • Long-term commitment

Each written response must be 1,500 characters (approximately 300 words) or less.

Applicants will also provide a one-minute video response discussing something they have remained committed to over a long period of time, or explaining why they want the fellowship to become their first long-term commitment.

How to Apply

Interested students should complete the online application before the deadline.

Application Deadline: September 4, 2026 at 11:59 PM PST

Application Link: Civic Innovators Fellowship 2026-2027 

Applicants are encouraged to prepare their responses in a separate document before submitting them through the application form.

For more information about Civics Unplugged and the Civic Innovators Fellowship, visit the official programme website.

Important Information for Applicants

Applicants should carefully consider the required time commitment before applying. Weekly live lessons take place every Monday at 7:30 PM ET, and attendance is required.

International applicants are welcome, but should remember that the fellowship is delivered in English and focuses substantially on the U.S. civic context.

The programme is particularly suited to students who are curious, proactive and interested in using their ideas and skills to address challenges in their communities.

Conclusion

The Civic Innovators Fellowship 2026–2027 offers high school students an opportunity to develop civic leadership skills, connect with a community of like-minded young people and gain practical experience in creating positive change.

With free participation, virtual learning, peer and alumni networks, access to funding and project opportunities, and exclusive post-fellowship programmes, CIF can provide a strong foundation for young people interested in civic innovation and community impact.

If you are a high school student or an eligible first-year gap student who is ready to take action and contribute to your community, consider applying before the September 4, 2026 deadline.

Discover more fellowship opportunities like this HERE.

item.content:encoded:
The Climate Vulnerable Forum (CVF) and V20 Finance Ministers are inviting applications for a range of senior professional positions within the CVF-V20 Secretariat. The opportunities span strategic communications, sovereign investment research and design, economics, climate finance, grants management, development finance, public investment, and international financial policy.

These positions offer experienced professionals an opportunity to contribute to international efforts focused on climate justice, climate finance, economic resilience, sovereign investment, disaster risk financing, development finance, and the broader transformation of financial systems serving climate-vulnerable countries.

The vacancies announced on 13 August 2026 include:

  1. Sovereign Investment Research & Design Director
  2. Sovereign Investment Research & Design Lead Economist
  3. Director of Communications
  4. Grants Management Specialist

Each position has a different area of responsibility and experience requirement, but all four roles are connected to the CVF-V20’s wider mission of strengthening climate resilience, mobilizing finance, advancing economic transformation, and improving access to financial resources for vulnerable economies.

About the Climate Vulnerable Forum and V20

The Climate Vulnerable Forum (CVF) was founded in 2009 as an independent intergovernmental organization representing countries that are particularly vulnerable to the impacts of climate change. According to the vacancy information, the CVF is headquartered in Accra, Ghana, and brings together leaders from 70 governments across Africa, Asia, the Caribbean, Latin America, and the Pacific, collectively representing approximately 1.74 billion people.

The V20 Finance Ministers were established in 2015 as a dedicated international collaboration of finance ministers and, in some countries, economic planning ministers. The V20 works to address climate change by mobilizing economic and development strategies and leveraging public and private finance.

The V20 also established a Central Bank Governors Working Group in 2023, focusing on areas including:

  • Liquidity support.
  • Inclusive green finance.
  • The role of central banks in greening the financial system.

Another important component of the CVF-V20 structure is the Global Parliamentary Group (GPG), founded in 2022. The group supports climate action and green industrial policy while helping promote long-term reforms and investment opportunities through Climate Prosperity Plans.

Together, the CVF-V20 works toward climate justice through Climate Prosperity Plans, economic and financial resilience strategies, and initiatives designed to mobilize investment and resources supporting the Sustainable Development Goals, global biodiversity objectives, and the goal of keeping global warming within the 1.5°C threshold established under the Paris Agreement.

About the CVF-V20 Secretariat

The CVF-V20 Secretariat supports the work of the CVF and V20 Finance Ministers by advancing their objectives and coordinating technical, diplomatic, financial, communications, and institutional activities.

Its responsibilities include supporting member-state convenings at the heads-of-state and ministerial levels, coordinating international meetings, representing CVF perspectives in international forums, providing technical assistance, supporting climate finance access, and engaging with governments, international financial institutions, investors, development partners, businesses, civil society organizations, and other stakeholders.

The Secretariat also works on:

  • International financial reform.
  • Climate finance.
  • Adaptation and mitigation.
  • Loss and damage finance.
  • Economic resilience.
  • Debt sustainability.
  • Access to development finance.
  • Financial instruments for vulnerable economies.
  • Climate Prosperity Plans.
  • Green industrial development.
  • Global financial safety-net reform.
  • Capacity building for member countries.

The four vacancies highlighted in this recruitment round contribute to different parts of this broad agenda.

1. Sovereign Investment Research & Design Director

The Sovereign Investment Research & Design Director will provide senior leadership to a unit responsible for two major functions: designing member-owned sovereign investment institutions and developing investment intelligence concerning green industrial opportunities across member economies.

This is a strategic senior-level role for a professional with substantial experience in sovereign funds, development finance institutions, finance ministries, public capital, investment vehicles, and international partnerships.

Objective of the Role

The Director will lead the Secretariat’s work relating to sovereign investment institutions and investment intelligence.

A major responsibility will be leading the design of the Multi-Sovereign Investment Fund while also overseeing the Secretariat’s contribution to the investment intelligence programme being delivered with specialized analytical partners.

The successful candidate will be expected to build and manage relationships with key internal and external stakeholders while coordinating resources and workflows between the investment design and intelligence functions.

The ultimate objective is to ensure that the Unit’s work produces practical outputs that can be used by V20 member governments, the Secretariat, and the Deal Team.

Key Responsibilities

A. Designing the Multi-Sovereign Investment Fund

The Director will lead the design of the proposed Fund, including:

  • Developing the investment thesis.
  • Determining sectoral priorities.
  • Designing governance arrangements.
  • Developing the capital structure.
  • Establishing the terms under which member states may participate.
  • Developing participation arrangements for development finance partners.
  • Convening participating member-state delegates.
  • Engaging key partners throughout the design process.
  • Ensuring continuous consultation with participating governments.
  • Aligning the Fund with the V2V Compact.
  • Ensuring that commitments under the Compact and the Fund’s capital structure reinforce one another.
  • Completing the Fund’s design proposal.
  • Building political and institutional support among member states.
  • Preparing a capitalization strategy.

The successful Director will therefore need to understand not only investment structures but also the political, institutional, and development considerations involved in creating a pooled sovereign investment vehicle.

B. Leading Investment Intelligence

The Director will also shape and oversee the Unit’s investment intelligence programme.

This includes working with the Managing Director and member states to determine:

  • Intelligence requirements.
  • Priority geographic markets.
  • Research priorities.
  • Programme sequencing.
  • Information needs.
  • Analytical requirements.

The Director will represent the Secretariat and member states when procuring and managing specialized partners responsible for supplying data, information, and analytical infrastructure.

Member-state consultation will remain an important component of the work to ensure that intelligence products respond to the most important questions facing governments.

C. Partnerships and Member Engagement

The Director will manage relationships with sovereign development funds and engage these institutions as potential:

  • Investors.
  • Co-investors.
  • Strategic partners.
  • Counterparties.

The Director will also be responsible for delivering the Sovereign Green Development Roundtable in Bangkok on 13 October 2026 and its successor planned for April 2027 in Washington.

The role will also include leadership of the research programme associated with these convenings.

In addition, the Director will support the Managing Director in raising the funding required to sustain the Unit beyond its initial term.

Qualifications and Experience

Applicants for the Sovereign Investment Research & Design Director position should have:

  • Substantial senior-level professional experience involving sovereign funds, development finance institutions, and finance ministries.
  • Experience with the governance and deployment of public capital for development.
  • A proven record of designing sovereign investment vehicles.
  • Experience convening sovereign funds, DFIs, philanthropic organizations, and other partners around pooled investment structures.
  • Established relationships with development-mandated sovereign funds in Africa, Asia, and Latin America.
  • Established relationships within CVF-V20 membership and its development finance partners.
  • Experience directing applied research and analytical programmes.
  • Experience involving industrial strategy, value chains, and public investment.
  • An advanced degree in a relevant discipline.
  • Working fluency in multiple V20 member languages.

2. Sovereign Investment Research & Design Lead Economist

The Sovereign Investment Research & Design Lead Economist will lead the Unit’s research and analytical activities.

The position serves as the Secretariat’s analytical counterpart to specialized partners responsible for providing data, information, and analytical infrastructure.

The Lead Economist will produce the research supporting the Multi-Sovereign Investment Fund and will serve as the principal author of the Unit’s published research.

Objective of the Role

The Lead Economist will be responsible for ensuring that the Unit’s investment intelligence is technically rigorous, relevant to member-state priorities, and converted into actionable research.

The position combines economic research, investment analysis, public finance, sovereign investment, industrial strategy, and policy communication.

Key Responsibilities

A. Investment Intelligence

The Lead Economist will own and manage the technical architecture of the intelligence programme.

Responsibilities include:

  • Setting standards for data and analytical services supplied by specialized partners.
  • Ensuring that external analytical inputs align with member-state priorities.
  • Turning information and data into actionable research products.
  • Supporting the V20 membership, Secretariat, and Deal Team.
  • Coordinating with the Deal Team to determine how analytical outputs can support market screening.
  • Supporting evaluation of investment markets and opportunities.
  • Providing intelligence and analysis for member-state consultations.

This means the successful candidate will need strong analytical skills as well as the ability to translate complex research into practical information for government and investment decision-makers.

B. Fund and Compact Analysis

The Lead Economist will produce research supporting the design and investment strategy of the Multi-Sovereign Investment Fund.

This includes analysis of:

  • Capitalization.
  • Capital structure.
  • Fund mandate.
  • Fund scope.
  • Risk-return allocation.
  • Public capital deployment.
  • Investment priorities.
  • The relationship between the Fund and the Compact.

The Lead Economist will also assess where public capital can potentially have the greatest development and investment impact across the Fund and the Compact.

C. Research and Publications

The successful candidate will have lead authorship responsibility for the Unit’s research output.

This includes research examining development-mandated sovereign funds to support the Bangkok and Washington convenings.

The Lead Economist will also:

  • Prepare research materials for member states.
  • Prepare materials for the Board.
  • Prepare research for development finance partners.
  • Represent the Unit in public forums.
  • Translate complex economic and investment issues into high-quality research publications.

Qualifications and Experience

Applicants should possess:

  • Substantial professional experience involving sovereign funds, development finance institutions, and finance ministries.
  • Experience in the governance and deployment of public capital for development.
  • A proven record designing sovereign investment vehicles.
  • Experience convening sovereign funds, DFIs, philanthropic partners, and other stakeholders around pooled structures.
  • Established relationships across development-mandated sovereign funds in Africa, Asia, and Latin America.
  • Strong relationships within CVF-V20 membership and its development finance partners.
  • Experience directing applied research and analytical programmes.
  • Expertise in industrial strategy, value chains, and public investment.
  • An advanced degree in a relevant field.
  • Working fluency in multiple V20 member languages.

3. Director of Communications

The Director of Communications is responsible for leading the CVF-V20’s global communications strategy and communications practice.

This is a particularly senior communications position that combines strategic communications leadership with hands-on editorial, media, digital, crisis communications, and campaign responsibilities.

The Director will serve as the principal communications adviser to the institution and will hold editorial leadership over its external voice.

Why Communications Is Important to the CVF-V20

The CVF-V20’s work covers highly complex issues such as:

  • Climate Prosperity Plans.
  • The V20-DFI Compact.
  • Cost of capital.
  • Credit ratings.
  • Sovereign debt.
  • Liquidity.
  • Debt sustainability.
  • Adaptation finance.
  • Loss and damage finance.
  • International financial reform.
  • Climate finance.
  • Green industrial development.

The Director of Communications will be responsible for transforming this analytical and diplomatic work into clear narratives that can generate political traction among governments, international financial institutions, investors, development partners, media organizations, and the wider public.

The position therefore requires someone who can operate both as a strategic communications leader and a hands-on communications practitioner.

Key Responsibilities

A. Develop the Global Communications Strategy

The Director will establish and own the CVF-V20 global communications strategy.

This includes determining:

  • Core narratives.
  • Priority audiences.
  • Communications channels.
  • Annual campaigns.
  • Media priorities.
  • Digital strategy.
  • Major communications moments.

The strategy will be anchored around major international events, including:

  • United Nations General Assembly.
  • UNFCCC Conferences of the Parties.
  • World Bank Group meetings.
  • International Monetary Fund meetings.
  • G20 processes.
  • G7 processes.
  • CVF-V20 Leaders’ meetings.
  • CVF-V20 Ministerial meetings.

B. Maintain the Messaging Architecture

The Director will maintain a unified messaging framework covering the CVF-V20’s major policy priorities.

These include:

  • Climate Prosperity Plans.
  • The V20-DFI Compact.
  • Country platforms.
  • Cost of capital.
  • Credit ratings.
  • Liquidity.
  • Debt sustainability.
  • Adaptation.
  • Loss and damage.

The objective is to ensure that speeches, publications, campaigns, policy products, media statements, and digital content communicate a coherent institutional narrative.

C. Provide Senior Communications Advice

The Director will advise institutional leadership on:

  • Positioning.
  • Timing of announcements.
  • Communications platforms.
  • Reputational risks.
  • Media opportunities.
  • Strategic communications decisions.
  • Whether particular opportunities should be accepted or declined.

This will require excellent political judgment and the ability to operate confidently in sensitive international policy environments.

D. Editorial Leadership

The Director will provide final editorial oversight of the organization’s external communications.

This includes:

  • Press releases.
  • Official statements.
  • Op-eds.
  • Policy briefs.
  • Website content.
  • Flagship publications.
  • Campaign materials.
  • Institutional communications.

The successful candidate must ensure that all external products meet high standards of accuracy, consistency, clarity, and quality.

E. International Media Relations

The Director will lead the organization’s global media strategy.

Responsibilities include developing relationships with:

  • Senior international editors.
  • International correspondents.
  • Regional media organizations.
  • Media outlets across Africa.
  • Media outlets across Asia.
  • Caribbean media.
  • Latin American media.
  • Pacific media.

The Director will also place institutional principals for interviews, commentary, and briefings and lead press operations during summits and ministerial meetings.

F. Build and Manage the Communications Team

The Director will build and mentor a lean, high-performing communications team.

Responsibilities include:

  • Recruitment.
  • Work planning.
  • Performance management.
  • Professional standards.
  • Team development.
  • Agency management.
  • Consultant management.

External service providers may include agencies and consultants supporting:

  • Design.
  • Digital communications.
  • Film and video.
  • Translation.
  • Media services.

Despite the leadership nature of the role, the successful candidate will also be expected to personally draft and produce communications products.

G. Coordinate Communications with Member States

The Director will work with member governments and support communications teams associated with the:

  • Presidency.
  • Chair.
  • Troika.
  • Member-country focal points.

This coordination will help ensure that Secretariat communications and member-state communications reinforce each other.

The Director will also support member-led events such as Climate Prosperity Plan launches and country-platform announcements.

H. Manage Partner Communications

The Director will lead joint communications with:

  • Multilateral development banks.
  • United Nations agencies and systems.
  • Climate funds.
  • Philanthropic organizations.
  • Civil society organizations.
  • Allied international groupings.

The goal is to secure strong CVF-V20 positioning while maintaining the organization’s independent institutional voice.

I. Manage the Brand and Digital Estate

The Director will own the CVF-V20 brand and digital presence, including:

  • Visual identity.
  • House style.
  • Website.
  • Digital platforms.
  • Publication standards.
  • Social media channels.
  • Digital audience growth.

Where practical, communications should be produced in languages relevant to member constituencies.

J. Communications Measurement

The Director will establish a measurement framework and report results to the Chief Executive Officer.

Performance measurement will include:

  • Reach.
  • Share of voice.
  • Message pull-through.
  • Policy outcomes.
  • Media outcomes.
  • Audience engagement.

The Director will use evidence and analytics to continually improve the communications strategy.

K. Crisis and Reputational Communications

The position will also lead crisis and reputational risk communications.

This includes maintaining:

  • Escalation procedures.
  • Prepared response lines.
  • Rapid-response capacity.
  • Crisis communications protocols.

The Director will advise leadership during sensitive or politically contested situations.

Qualifications for the Director of Communications

The position requires a particularly strong combination of education, communications leadership, media experience, political judgment, and international policy knowledge.

Applicants should have:

  1. A Master’s degree in communications, journalism, international relations, public policy, political science, development, or a related field. A Bachelor’s degree combined with extensive relevant experience may be accepted instead.
  2. At least 10 years of progressively responsible communications experience.
  3. At least 3 years leading a communications function or team in an international or intergovernmental organization, government, financial institution, major foundation, NGO, or media organization.
  4. A proven record of developing and implementing communications strategies that influenced policy debates or achieved defined institutional objectives.
  5. Senior-level media relations experience and established relationships with leading editors and correspondents.
  6. Experience securing media coverage in Global South markets.
  7. Strong knowledge of climate finance, sovereign debt, cost of capital, adaptation, loss and damage, and the international financial architecture.
  8. Experience advising heads of state, ministers, chief executives, or other senior principals.
  9. Speechwriting and real-time communications advisory experience in high-pressure environments.
  10. Experience leading communications or press operations during major international events.
  11. Experience building and managing teams and budgets.
  12. Experience directing external agencies and consultants.
  13. Ability to personally draft, edit, and produce publication-ready communications.
  14. Experience working with climate-vulnerable countries across Africa, Asia, the Caribbean, Latin America, and the Pacific.
  15. Excellent written and spoken English.
  16. French, Spanish, Arabic, or Portuguese proficiency is an advantage.
  17. Strong digital communications skills.
  18. Experience with audience analytics, social media, web content management, video, and design workflows.
  19. Strong political judgment, discretion, and confidentiality.
  20. Ability to work under pressure and across multiple time zones.
  21. Willingness and ability to travel internationally frequently.

4. Grants Management Specialist

The Grants Management Specialist will support the CVF-V20 Secretariat’s grant management, donor reporting, compliance, financial tracking, and programme accountability functions.

The role is particularly connected to the CVF-V20’s efforts to strengthen the global financial safety net, expand pre-arranged disaster risk financing, and address financial protection gaps in vulnerable economies.

A major component of the position involves the V20 Funding Program, which is funded by the Global Environment Facility (GEF), with the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO) serving as the implementing partner.

Objective of the Role

The Grants Management Specialist will provide technical, financial, operational, and administrative support to ensure that funds received from donors, vertical funds, and multilateral partners are managed transparently, effectively, and in compliance with applicable requirements.

The successful candidate will oversee important parts of the grant lifecycle, donor compliance processes, programme monitoring, and reporting.

The position reports directly to the Deputy Director, Financial Protection and Vertical Funds.

Key Responsibilities

A. Donor Reporting

The Specialist will lead the drafting, consolidation, and quality assurance of:

  • Periodic donor reports.
  • Quarterly financial assessments.
  • Annual financial assessments.
  • Technical progress reports.
  • Terminal evaluations.

The candidate will work within GEF and UNIDO reporting frameworks.

B. Grant Oversight

The Specialist will serve as the primary technical focal point for grant oversight under the GEF-funded and UNIDO-implemented V20 Funding Program.

Responsibilities include:

  • Tracking project milestones.
  • Managing sub-recipient agreements.
  • Monitoring implementation.
  • Supporting community-level implementation.
  • Working with lead implementing agencies.

C. Tracking Climate Finance

The Specialist will monitor and analyze funding flows involving major vertical climate funds, including:

  • Global Environment Facility.
  • Green Climate Fund.
  • Adaptation Fund.
  • Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage.

The Specialist will maintain a real-time tracking dashboard covering:

  • Fund flows.
  • Grant disbursements.
  • Financial protection gaps.

D. Disaster Risk Financing

The role also involves supporting financial and operational monitoring of:

  • Pre-arranged disaster risk financing products.
  • Microinsurance mechanisms.
  • Regional risk pools.
  • Other financial protection instruments for CVF-V20 member countries.

E. Research and Technical Briefs

The Specialist will contribute to technical publications addressing:

  • Pre-arranged financing.
  • Disaster risk financing.
  • Regional financial protection mechanisms.
  • Climate finance.
  • Loss and damage financing.

This will require the ability to interpret technical financial information and communicate it clearly to decision-makers.

F. Training and Workshops

The Specialist will design and coordinate technical workshops for member-state officials and implementation agencies.

These workshops will focus on:

  • Tracking climate finance.
  • Managing climate finance.
  • Reporting climate finance.
  • Strengthening financial accountability.
  • Improving grant management.

G. Executive Reporting

The position will prepare:

  • Financial summaries.
  • Grant portfolio updates.
  • Executive briefing notes.

These materials will support senior leadership ahead of major international events, including:

  • COP.
  • United Nations General Assembly.
  • World Bank meetings.
  • IMF meetings.

H. Compliance and Audit Readiness

The Specialist will maintain strong compliance with:

  • Organizational policies.
  • UN agency requirements.
  • Donor requirements.
  • Monitoring frameworks.
  • Evaluation requirements.
  • Audit-readiness standards.

The position may also undertake additional responsibilities assigned by the Deputy Director for Financial Protection and Vertical Funds.

Qualifications and Experience

Applicants for the Grants Management Specialist role should have:

  • A Master’s degree in Business Administration, Public Finance, Economics, Climate Policy, Environmental Economics, or a closely related field.
  • At least 7 years of progressive professional experience in grant management, climate finance delivery, disaster risk financing, or international donor compliance.
  • Proven experience managing complete grant lifecycles.
  • Experience establishing risk-based monitoring frameworks.
  • Experience managing sub-recipient agreements.
  • Experience producing compliant donor reports for major international donors and UN agencies.
  • Specific knowledge of GEF and UNIDO standards.
  • Technical knowledge of the operational policies and access requirements of major vertical funds.
  • Knowledge of GEF, GCF, Adaptation Fund, and Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage mechanisms.
  • Experience with pre-arranged disaster financing instruments.
  • Direct experience supporting or overseeing community-level Loss and Damage or climate adaptation grants.
  • Excellent technical drafting skills in English.
  • Ability to convert complex quantitative and financial information into executive-level reports.
  • Cultural sensitivity when working with governments, donors, and implementation partners across CVF-V20 regions.
  • An entrepreneurial, adaptive, and collaborative approach.
  • Fluency in English.
  • Additional regional language skills are an advantage.

Application Requirements for the CVF-V20 Vacancies

Candidates applying for these positions should pay close attention to the required application materials.

For the positions described above, applicants are required to submit:

  • A curriculum vitae (CV).
  • A cover letter.
  • The names of two professional referees.

Applications should be submitted to the CVF-V20 Secretariat using the email address provided in the vacancy announcement:

hr@cvfv20.org

Because the vacancies have different closing dates, applicants should ensure that they submit their applications before the deadline applicable to the specific position.

CVF-V20 Job Deadlines

The application deadlines are as follows:

Position Deadline
Sovereign Investment Research & Design Director 30 August 2026
Sovereign Investment Research & Design Lead Economist 30 August 2026
Director of Communications 13 September 2026
Grants Management Specialist 15 September 2026

Applicants should avoid waiting until the final day to submit their applications, particularly where a CV, cover letter, and professional referee information are required.

Who Should Apply?

These vacancies are primarily aimed at experienced and senior professionals, rather than students or early-career applicants.

The ideal applicants will generally fall into one or more of the following professional categories:

  • Senior communications professionals.
  • International development professionals.
  • Sovereign investment specialists.
  • Economists.
  • Development finance professionals.
  • Public finance specialists.
  • Climate finance experts.
  • Grant management professionals.
  • Disaster risk financing specialists.
  • International policy experts.
  • Public investment specialists.
  • Financial sector professionals.
  • Government and ministry professionals.
  • Professionals with experience in sovereign wealth or development-mandated funds.
  • Professionals with experience working with multilateral development banks.
  • Professionals with experience working with international donors and vertical climate funds.
  • Professionals with extensive experience in international or intergovernmental organizations.

The positions generally require advanced degrees and significant professional experience, making them particularly suitable for established professionals seeking senior international roles.

Geographic Eligibility and Regional Experience

The vacancy information does not specify a particular nationality, race, or citizenship requirement for applicants.

Therefore, the available information does not establish that applicants must belong to a particular racial group or hold citizenship from a specific country.

However, regional experience is highly relevant.

The CVF-V20 represents countries and governments across:

  • Africa
  • Asia
  • The Caribbean
  • Latin America
  • The Pacific

Several positions specifically request experience or relationships involving these regions.

For example, the Sovereign Investment Research & Design positions seek established relationships across development-mandated sovereign funds in Africa, Asia, and Latin America, while the Director of Communications position specifically requires experience working in or with climate-vulnerable countries across Africa, Asia, the Caribbean, Latin America, and the Pacific.

The Grants Management Specialist position similarly emphasizes cultural sensitivity and the ability to work with government officials, donors, and implementation partners across these CVF-V20 regions.

Consequently, international applicants from any region may be considered if they satisfy the relevant requirements, but candidates with demonstrated experience working across CVF-V20 member regions may be particularly competitive.

Why These CVF-V20 Opportunities Are Significant

These vacancies are significant because they sit at the intersection of climate policy, international finance, economic development, sovereign investment, communications, and financial resilience.

The roles provide opportunities to contribute to initiatives addressing some of the most important financial challenges facing climate-vulnerable economies.

Professionals appointed to these positions could contribute to areas such as:

  • Mobilizing public and private capital.
  • Strengthening climate finance access.
  • Developing sovereign investment structures.
  • Improving disaster risk financing.
  • Supporting climate adaptation.
  • Addressing loss and damage financing.
  • Strengthening economic resilience.
  • Improving international financial cooperation.
  • Advancing green industrial strategies.
  • Communicating climate-finance priorities to global audiences.
  • Strengthening donor accountability.
  • Supporting governments in accessing and managing climate finance.

The combination of policy, finance, research, communications, and international engagement makes these roles particularly relevant for professionals interested in the intersection between climate change and global economic governance.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

Because these are senior professional positions, applicants should avoid submitting generic application documents.

1. Tailor Your CV

Your CV should clearly demonstrate the experience requested for the specific position.

For example:

  • Communications applicants should emphasize international communications strategy, media relations, crisis communications, campaign leadership, digital communications, and advisory work.
  • Sovereign investment applicants should highlight sovereign funds, DFIs, public capital, investment vehicles, pooled structures, and government relationships.
  • Lead Economist applicants should emphasize economic research, investment analysis, industrial strategy, public investment, and analytical programmes.
  • Grants Management applicants should emphasize donor compliance, grant lifecycle management, climate finance, reporting, financial monitoring, and vertical funds.

2. Demonstrate Results

Senior positions require evidence of impact rather than simply listing responsibilities.

Where possible, candidates should demonstrate:

  • What they were responsible for.
  • The scale of the programme.
  • The stakeholders involved.
  • The problem they addressed.
  • The action they took.
  • The measurable result.

3. Prepare a Targeted Cover Letter

The cover letter should explain why the candidate is suitable for the specific CVF-V20 position.

It should connect previous experience to the responsibilities outlined in the vacancy rather than simply repeating the CV.

4. Highlight International Experience

Given the international nature of the CVF-V20, candidates should clearly demonstrate experience working with:

  • Governments.
  • Finance ministries.
  • International organizations.
  • Development finance institutions.
  • Donors.
  • Multilateral development banks.
  • Climate funds.
  • International media.
  • Civil society.
  • Private-sector stakeholders.

5. Prepare Professional Referees

Each application requires the names of two professional referees.

Candidates should select referees who can credibly speak about their professional capabilities, leadership, technical expertise, and relevant experience.

Important Dates at a Glance

The vacancies were announced on 13 August 2026.

30 August 2026

Deadline for:

  • Sovereign Investment Research & Design Director.
  • Sovereign Investment Research & Design Lead Economist.

13 September 2026

Deadline for:

  • Director of Communications.

15 September 2026

Deadline for:

  • Grants Management Specialist.

Applicants should verify all application details before submission and ensure their documents reach the CVF-V20 Secretariat before the relevant deadline.

Visit HERE to learn more about the CVF-V20 Jobs 2026

Final Takeaway

The CVF-V20 2026 recruitment opportunities provide experienced professionals with the chance to contribute to international efforts addressing climate vulnerability, financial resilience, sovereign investment, climate finance, economic transformation, and global communications.

The Sovereign Investment Research & Design Director and Lead Economist positions are particularly suited to professionals with substantial expertise in sovereign investment, development finance, public capital, economic research, and government relationships.

The Director of Communications position is aimed at a highly experienced communications leader capable of shaping global narratives, managing international media relationships, advising senior political leaders, leading communications teams, and communicating complex climate and financial issues to diverse audiences.

The Grants Management Specialist role is designed for an experienced grant and climate-finance professional capable of managing donor requirements, financial reporting, compliance, climate-finance flows, and disaster risk financing programmes.

With deadlines ranging from 30 August to 15 September 2026, qualified professionals should begin preparing their applications early. A strong, tailored CV, a focused cover letter, and appropriate professional referees will be essential components of the application.

For professionals seeking to build or advance an international career at the intersection of climate action, finance, economic development, sovereign investment, communications, and global policy, these CVF-V20 positions represent significant opportunities to contribute to initiatives affecting climate-vulnerable economies across Africa, Asia, the Caribbean, Latin America, and the Pacific.
